newsitem.title: CANADA: Lumber industry seen new source of flax demand - ADM.
newsitem.headline: Lumber industry seen new source of flax demand - ADM.

text.p: A flaxseed oil-based glue for composite wood products is creating a modest new source of demand for the oilseed in the next three years, an Archer Daniels Midland Co official said.

"We can expect ADM will need to procure more flax (for the lumber industry)," said Michelle Vandevoorde, flaxseed merchandising manager at ADM's Red Wing, Minn., crushing plant. "Let's theorize demand will reach 26 million lbs (12 million kg) in the next three years."
About 30,000 tonnes of flax would have to be crushed to produce 12 million kg of modified linseed oil resin, Vandevoorde told Flax Council of Canada members meeting here.
ADM targeted the oriented strand board sector for its newly-developed flax-based bonding agent because it holds the most growth potential in the lumber industry, she said.
North American production of oriented strand board reached 11 billion square feet in 1995 and was projected to reach 33 billion square feet by the year 2000, Vandevoorde said.
Processors use resins such as liquid fenal formaldehyde and other bonding agents to glue strands of woods into panels used in roofing and wall sheeting.
The cost of traditional resins range from US$0.75-$0.90 a lb while flax resin is costs US$0.42 to $0.45 a lb, she said.
Louisiana-Pacific Corp and Potlatch Corp tested the flax resin, Vandevoorde said, and Weyerhaeuser Canada Ltd will test it at its plant in Edson, Alta., next week.

Test results at an average plant with an annual output of 500 million square feet a year where 25 percent of the bonding agents used was flax resin, showed little to no variation in board strength, Vandevoorde said.

The North American oriented strand board sector spends about US$5.2 million on resins each year and could save US$625,000, or 12 percent, if 25 percent of its purchases were of lower-priced flax-based resins, she added.
